h1: The 7 Best Ultrasonic Cleaners Under $100 for Jewelry, Glasses and Retainers, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 ultrasonic cleaners under $100 compared on tank size, frequency, degassing, heater and gentle mode for jewelry and retainers.
summary: The VEVOR 2L is the ultrasonic cleaner to buy first, because it pairs a 2 liter tank with 60W, a gentle mode and upgraded degassing for under $50. The CREWORKS 2L with a 150W heater and a 1 to 30 minute timer is the pick for grimy tools and watch bracelets, while the iSonic F3900 is the only unit here built around retainers and aligners. The compact KUNPHY and Miorcols pods suit a single ring and a bathroom shelf, not a workbench.
intro: Most people shop for an ultrasonic cleaner by wattage, and that is the first mistake. A bigger number on the box says little about how well the tank cleans a ring. What decides the result is the frequency, whether the water has been degassed, and whether the unit gives you a gentle setting for soft stones and plastic. A 60W machine with proper degassing will beat a louder, rougher one that pushes air bubbles around instead of collapsing them against the metal.

This ranking covers seven cleaners that sell under $100, from a compact 12 ounce pod to 2 liter digital baths with heaters and timers. We reviewed spec sheets and listings for tank size, frequency, power, heater, timer, degas and gentle modes, then ranked them by how much practical capability each one gives you per dollar. Where a listing does not state a figure, we leave it out rather than guess.

products.name: VEVOR 2L Ultrasonic Cleaner
products.verdict: A 2 liter, 60W, 40kHz cleaner with degassing and a gentle mode for under $50.
products.description:
The VEVOR is a 2 liter digital cleaner rated at 60W and 40kHz, with a heater, a timer, an upgraded degassing function and a gentle mode. That list matches what the dearer units here offer, yet the price stays below $50.

The VEVOR leads since the features that matter for real cleaning are all present. Degassing runs the transducer before you load anything, driving dissolved air out of the water so cavitation bubbles form and collapse cleanly instead of cushioning the work. The gentle mode drops the intensity, which is what you want for softer gemstones, plated pieces and plastic. Against the CREWORKS units below it, the listing gives no heater wattage or timer range, so you are trusting the general spec.

Buy it if you want one machine that handles rings, glasses, watch bands and small tools. Skip it if you need a published timer range or a heater figure before you commit.
pros: Degassing and gentle mode both included
products.idealFor: Households that clean jewelry, glasses and small tools in one machine.
products.skipIf: You want a stated heater output and timer range.

products.name: CREWORKS 2L Digital Ultrasonic Cleaner with 150W Heater
products.verdict: The most clearly specified 2L unit: 150W heater, 1 to 30 minute timer, degas and gentle modes.
products.description:
This CREWORKS pairs a 2 liter (0.5 gallon) tank with a 60W ultrasonic output, a separate 150W heater and a timer that runs from 1 to 30 minutes. Degas and gentle modes are both on the panel.

Heat is the reason to rank it second and not lower. Warm water loosens oils, sunscreen residue and greasy film faster than cold water, so a heated bath shortens cycles on watch bracelets, eyeglass frames and tools. The 150W figure is the heating element, not the cleaning power, which is a distinction many listings blur. It sits behind the VEVOR only because it costs more for a similar cleaning core, and it lands in the $50 to $100 bracket.

Choose it for dirty tools, razor heads and metal parts where heat and a long timer earn their keep. Skip it if you mainly clean a few rings a month, because the VEVOR does that for less.
pros: Suited to tools and watch bands
cons: Heat can harm some plated finishes
products.idealFor: Anyone cleaning greasy tools, bracelets and eyeglass frames regularly.
products.skipIf: You only clean a ring or two and never need heat.

products.name: CREWORKS 2L Digital Ultrasonic Cleaning Machine
products.verdict: A 60W digital cleaner with heater, timer, degas and gentle mode, marketed to retainer and denture owners.
products.description:
This model carries a 2 liter tank, 60W ultrasonic power, a heater and timer, and both degas and gentle modes. Its listing names retainers, watches, dentures and glasses among the intended uses.

It ranks third because it matches the specs of the units above without improving on them. The gentle mode is the useful part for dental appliances, since acrylic and thin wire clasps do better at reduced intensity than at full blast. Compared with the 150W heater model, this listing does not publish a heater figure or timer range, so it reads as the plainer of the two CREWORKS machines for a similar price.

It makes sense for households with a retainer, a night guard and a few pairs of glasses sharing one cleaner. Skip it if you want the extra clarity of the model above or the lower cost of the VEVOR.
pros: Digital panel with timer and heater
products.idealFor: Families sharing one cleaner across retainers, watches and glasses.
products.skipIf: You want the lowest price in the 2L class.

products.name: CREWORKS 2L Jewelry Cleaning Machine 40kHz
products.verdict: A no-frills 2 liter, 40kHz digital bath for batches of rings, chains and small parts.
products.description:
This is the older-style CREWORKS: a 2 liter tank, 40kHz frequency and digital sonic controls, priced in the $25 to $50 bracket. The listing does not mention degassing or a gentle mode.

That gap is why it ranks below the VEVOR despite the same tank size. Without a degas function you have to run the machine empty for a few minutes and let the water settle, which works but takes patience. With no gentle setting, soft stones such as opals, pearls and emeralds should stay out of the tank. Where it earns its place is batch work: the 2 liter basin takes several chains, a few rings or a handful of small parts at once.

Buy it if you clean durable metals and hard stones and want the bigger basket. Skip it if your collection includes porous or treated stones.
products.idealFor: Owners of durable gold, silver and steel pieces who clean in batches.
products.skipIf: You wear opals, pearls or other soft stones.

products.name: iSonic F3900 Denture, Aligner and Retainer Cleaner
products.verdict: The only unit here built around dental appliances, with a box of cleaning tablets included.
products.description:
The F3900 is aimed squarely at dentures, aligners and retainers, and it ships with one box of AlignerClean ultrasonic cleaning tablets. It sits in the $25 to $50 bracket.

It ranks fifth because its focus is narrow. A dental-specific cleaner makes sense when the item is clear plastic that scratches easily, and a bundled tablet means you can start cleaning on day one without sourcing a solution. The listing gives no frequency or tank volume, so you cannot compare it against the 2 liter baths on capacity. Treat it as a bathroom-counter appliance for one person, not a workshop tool.

Pick it if aligners or a retainer are the whole reason you are buying. Skip it if you also want to clean watches, tools or a ring collection.
cons: No frequency or tank size listed
Too small for tools or bulk jewelry
products.idealFor: Aligner and retainer wearers who want a purpose-built cleaner.
products.skipIf: You want one machine for jewelry, glasses and tools.

products.name: Miorcols 48kHz Jewelry Ultrasonic Cleaner
products.verdict: A compact 304 stainless steel pod running at 48kHz for rings, watch straps and glasses.
products.description:
The Miorcols uses a 12 ounce cleaning pod made of 304 stainless steel and runs at 48kHz. The listing names jewelry, glasses, rings, retainers, watch straps and dentures as intended items, and it sits in the $25 to $50 bracket.

The higher frequency is the interesting part. A 48kHz output produces smaller cavitation bubbles than 40kHz, which tends to be gentler on delicate surfaces and good at fine crevices, though it is less aggressive on heavy deposits. It ranks sixth because 12 ounces limits you to a piece or two at a time and the listing mentions no heater, timer range or degas mode.

It suits someone who wants a small, matte black appliance for the occasional ring and pair of glasses. Skip it if you clean in volume or need a heater.
products.idealFor: Light users who clean one ring or a pair of glasses at a time.
products.skipIf: You clean several pieces per session or want a heater.

products.name: KUNPHY 46kHz Ultrasonic Jewelry Cleaner
products.verdict: A small, jewelry-focused 46kHz cleaner for the lowest-effort entry into ultrasonic cleaning.
products.description:
The KUNPHY runs at 46kHz in a compact white body, and its listing is jewelry-focused. It sells in the $25 to $50 bracket and offers fewer published details than any other unit here.

It lands last because the information gap is wide. There is no tank volume, power, timer, degas or gentle setting in the listing, so you are choosing it on frequency and size alone. The 46kHz output is a reasonable middle ground between standard 40kHz baths and 48kHz pods, and for a bedside dish of rings it should be adequate.

It is for a first-time buyer who wants to see what ultrasonic cleaning does before spending more. Skip it if you want documented features or any capacity beyond a few small pieces.
cons: No gentle or degas mode listed
products.idealFor: First-time buyers who only clean a few rings.
products.skipIf: You want documented power, timer or heater features.

whatMatters.detail: Frequency sets the size of the cavitation bubbles that scrub the surface. Around 40kHz is the common general-purpose figure, while 46kHz and 48kHz produce finer bubbles that are gentler and reach tighter crevices. Check the listing for a kHz number, because some give none at all.

Freshly poured water holds dissolved air, which absorbs ultrasonic energy and weakens cleaning. A degas function runs the transducer for a few minutes to drive that air out first. Look for the word degas, since a machine without it needs a manual empty run before each session.

Soft or porous stones, plated finishes and thin plastics can be damaged at full intensity. A gentle setting lowers the output for those items. Pearls, opals and emeralds should stay out of any ultrasonic bath regardless, so treat gentle mode as protection for hardier pieces.

Listings often quote two numbers that mean different things. The 60W figure is the ultrasonic output that does the scrubbing, and a number like 150W describes the water heater. Warm water helps with oils and grease, so look for both figures stated separately.

A 2 liter tank holds several items at once, while a 12 ounce pod suits one ring. A timer from 1 to 30 minutes lets you set short cycles for delicate pieces and longer ones for grimy parts. Match capacity to the largest item you plan to clean.

faq.q: Can I clean glasses with an ultrasonic cleaner?
faq.a: Yes, for most metal and plastic frames. Skip it if your lenses have an old or damaged coating, because vibration can worsen flaking. Use the gentle mode on the VEVOR or CREWORKS units and keep cycles short.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake with these machines?
faq.a: Putting items directly on the tank floor or using the wrong liquid. Use the basket, fill with water plus a small amount of detergent, and never run the unit dry. Soft stones like pearls and opals should never go in.

faq.q: Is the 150W heater model worth it over the VEVOR?
faq.a: Only if you clean greasy tools, bracelets or frames regularly. Warm water breaks down oils faster, and the CREWORKS publishes its timer range. For jewelry that is lightly soiled, the VEVOR does the same job for less.

faq.q: How do I set up a 2 liter cleaner?
faq.a: Fill the tank to the marked line with water and a drop of dish soap, switch on degas for a few minutes, then load the basket. Run a short cycle first and check progress before extending.

faq.q: How do I maintain the tank?
faq.a: Empty and rinse it after each use, and wipe the stainless surface dry. Mineral deposits from hard water can dull the finish over time, so distilled water helps if your tap water is hard.

faq.q: Can I use it for retainers every day?
faq.a: Many owners do a short cycle with a dental-safe tablet. The iSonic F3900 is designed for this routine. Avoid hot water on clear plastic, since heat can warp thin appliance material.

finalTake: The VEVOR 2L Ultrasonic Cleaner is the best buy under $100 for most homes, because it offers degassing, a gentle mode and a 2 liter tank at the lowest price in its class. Step up to the CREWORKS with the 150W heater if you clean greasy tools and want a published timer range. The iSonic F3900 is the dedicated pick for aligners, and the Miorcols and KUNPHY are fine for a ring or two. Match the machine to what you clean before you look at the price tag.
